# Research notes on Ezra 2:48–70

I couldn't find much for sections 2 and 3. I found nothing where Protestant traditions clearly disagree, and I didn't reach any Catholic, Orthodox, Bible Odyssey, NET Bible or prosperity-teaching pages on these verses. I left those out instead of guessing. Most of the notes below come from Enduring Word, Precept Austin, Bible.org and the older commentaries on BibleHub and StudyLight. Several of the BibleHub pages I used are "Commentaries" pages for a different verse, because they comment on nearby verses too.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 48–54 (the temple servants, or "Nethinim," continued)**
- Guzik thinks the Nethinim were probably descended from the Gibeonites of Joshua 9, who became servants of the priests and Levites. He quotes Trapp, who says their punishment for lying was to draw water for the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Kidner (quoted by Guzik) thinks they did the more menial jobs. He says some foreign-sounding names may point to people who came in after David's conquests, either as immigrants or as prisoners of war. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Precept Austin cites Edwin Yamauchi: about 68% of the temple servants' names are foreign. They may descend from David's prisoners of war or from the foreign groups Solomon used as forced labour (1 Kings 9:20–21). https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
- v. 51: Guzik says "Bakbuk" means "bottle." He suggests it was a nickname, for a big belly or for constant chatter like water gurgling from a bottle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

**vv. 55–57 (descendants of Solomon's servants)**
- Most commentators, says Guzik, see these as foreigners who worked for Solomon and joined Israel as converts. Trapp draws the lesson that "God is no respecter of persons." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Yamauchi (via Precept Austin) counts 33–40% of these names as foreign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 58 (total of 392)**
- Guzik treats the Nethinim and Solomon's servants as two special groups who came back together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Utley (Bible.org) says vv. 36–58 list the temple workers in order of importance: priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, then the special servants. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezra-2

**vv. 59–60 (the 652 who couldn't prove they were Israelites)**
- Precept Austin says ancestry still mattered. The 652 are singled out and seem to have been treated like circumcised foreigners. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
- Utley says proving your lineage was vital after the exile. It affected inheritance rights in Judah and a share in God's covenant promises. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezra-2
- Matthew Poole suggests the gap in the v. 64 total may partly be people who thought they were Israelites but couldn't prove it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm

**v. 61 (the priests: Hobaiah, Hakkoz, Barzillai)**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says the founder of the Barzillai family took that name because it seemed grander than being of Levi's house. That worldly ambition cost the family the priesthood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-62.htm
- Kidner (via Guzik) notes that Barzillai had been a rich supporter of David. Taking his name may have looked like giving up the birthright of the priesthood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Keil and Delitzsch say Hakkoz was the name of the seventh priestly division. Others had the same name, though, so the name alone proved nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-62.htm

**v. 62 (excluded as unclean)**
- The Cambridge Bible says they searched a priestly register known as "The Enrolled." Being declared "polluted" meant no active part in the priesthood until their claim was proved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-62.htm
- Gill says the Jews kept public records of priestly families. These men couldn't serve at the altar or receive priests' privileges. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-62.htm
- Matthew Henry says that in Babylon the priesthood earned nothing, so these families didn't keep up the connection. Now that the altar supported priests again, they wanted to be counted as priests. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-62.html
- Guzik sees this as admirable respect for God's law about the priesthood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- The BibleHub study notes say the exclusion didn't mean the men were morally guilty. It meant no one could take on holy duties without proper authority. https://biblehub.com/ezra/2-62.htm

**v. 63 (the governor, the most holy things, the Urim and Thummim)**
- **The governor ("Tirshatha"):** the Pulpit Commentary calls it Zerubbabel's Persian title, probably meaning "the Feared." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- Henry notes another view: the governor here is Nehemiah, who carries the same title in Nehemiah 8:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-63.html
- **The most holy things:** Benson lists the sin offerings, the right shoulder of the peace offerings, and the showbread, all kept for priests alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says these men were barred more strictly than a priest with a physical defect, who could still eat the holy food. They lost income as well as status. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch read it as a ban on specific priestly acts. It did not deny that they belonged to the priestly order in general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- Guzik and Henry both stress that this was a suspension, not a permanent ban. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-63.html
- **The Urim and Thummim:** Barnes says Zerubbabel seems to have expected their loss to be temporary. The rabbis say the second temple never had them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch link using them to God's presence at the ark, which no longer existed. There is no record of them being used after the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- **Pointing to Christ:** Gill cites a Talmudic saying that the phrase amounts to "until the dead rise, or the Messiah comes." He sees Christ as the true High Priest, "full of grace and truth." The Cambridge Bible likewise sees a longing for a coming great High Priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-63.htm
- Henry adds that they had the complete Old Testament, which was better than the Urim. Its absence taught them to look for the Messiah, of whom the Urim was only a type (a foreshadowing). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-63.html
- **A translation note:** the Douay-Rheims (Catholic) and the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) render the phrase differently, as "a priest learned and perfect" and "Lights and Perfections." https://biblehub.com/ezra/2-63.htm

**v. 64 (42,360, though the listed numbers add up to less)**
- **The problem:** the individual numbers total 29,818 in Ezra, 31,089 in Nehemiah 7 and 33,950 in 1 Esdras. All three give the same grand total. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm
- **Copying errors:** Ellicott, Barnes, the Cambridge Bible and Keil and Delitzsch prefer this explanation. Keil says the total is the same in all three texts, so it must be right. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm
- **Other tribes:** older Jewish and Christian writers (Rashi, Ussher), plus JFB, Henry and Gill's Jewish sources, think the extra people came from tribes other than Judah and Benjamin. Keil rejects this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm
- GotQuestions also prefers the other-tribes explanation. https://www.gotquestions.org/Ezra-Nehemiah-numbers.html
- **Omissions:** Constable quotes Breneman, who thinks some families were simply left out but the total is correct. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-64.html
- **How many people:** Guzik says this was only the first wave of returnees. He puts all who eventually returned at perhaps 100,000–150,000. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- Henry says that even this small group grew into a large nation by Roman times. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-64.html

**v. 65 (servants and singers)**
- Precept Austin works out about one slave for every six free people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
- Gaebelein says these 200 singers are a different group from the temple singers of vv. 41 and 70. He takes it that singing was prominent on the journey home. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezra-2.html

**vv. 66–67 (the animals)**
- Commentators disagree about what the animals show:
  - **Poverty:** the Pulpit Commentary reads them as a sign of poverty. It counts one donkey per six people, one horse per sixty, one camel per hundred. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm
  - **Wealth:** Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) sees God's mercy instead. The people went into exile with nothing and came back rich. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that such exact counts teach that nothing is too small for God to know. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-64.htm

**v. 68 (freewill offerings)**
- Henry notes that the temple was the first house they talked of building. They gave freely even though they had just finished a journey and were starting over. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ezr/Ezr_002.cfm
- Guzik draws the lesson that we should give sacrificially, according to our ability. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

**v. 69 (gold, silver and priests' garments)**
- Precept Austin, citing the Bible Knowledge Commentary, puts the gift at about 1,133 lbs of gold and 6,300 lbs of silver. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
- Clarke calls the daric a Persian gold coin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/2-69.html
- Ellicott thinks Nehemiah's smaller figures are probably more accurate. He suggests Ezra's 61,000 is a copying error for 41,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-69.htm
- Utley (Bible.org) says "according to their ability" later becomes a principle in Paul's letters. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezra-2
- Henry says their gifts were small next to those of David's princes, but just as acceptable, because they gave what they could. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
- The BibleHub study notes read the items as pictures: gold as Christ the King, silver as redemption, the garments as Christ's righteousness. https://biblehub.com/study/ezra/2-69.htm

**v. 70 (settling in their towns)**
- The Cambridge Bible says the people at first lived only in and around Jerusalem. Settling the towns took years, and the verse sums up a process that was long finished by the writer's time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-1.htm
- JFB and Benson give two possible meanings of "their own towns": the towns of their ancestors, or towns newly given to them, since many old towns lay in ruins or were occupied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-1.htm
- The ESV footnote says the Hebrew reads "all Israel." https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv/ezr/2/1/
- Kidner (via Precept Austin) says the chapter ends with the nation ordered and ready for its main purpose, worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no pages where traditions clearly disagree on these verses. Two Protestant applications came up:
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says Christianity has no exclusive priestly class. Every area of service is open to any Christian who is qualified for it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezra-2.html
- Henry applies v. 62 to believers today. Anyone without evidence of the new birth, which makes Christians "spiritual priests," has no right to Christian privileges. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-62.htm

## 3. Other views

I found nothing on these sites for modern scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox readings, or popular movements like prosperity teaching. The only related item is the Douay-Rheims wording in v. 63 above.
